desc:
A country has n towns labelled 0 to n - 1 and an existing set of two-way roads roads[i] = [a, b, w] of length w. The existing roads connect all towns (every town can reach every other). Two towns may be joined by several roads.

Then newRoads[j] = [a, b, w] are built one after another. After each new road is added (keeping all earlier roads and all earlier new roads), compute the sum, over all n(n - 1) / 2 unordered pairs of different towns, of the shortest route length between them. Return these sums as an array of length newRoads.length, one entry per construction.

Example: n = 4, roads = [[0,1,5],[1,2,5],[2,3,5]] and newRoads = [[0,3,4],[1,3,1]]. After the first new road the pair distances are 5, 5, 5, 9, 9, 4, which sum to 37. After the second, distances are 5, 1, 4, 5, 9, 5 which sum to 29. The answer is [37, 29].
constraints: n - 1 ≤ roads.length ≤ 500 and the existing roads connect all towns (for n = 1, roads is empty)
Every road has 0 ≤ a, b < n, a ≠ b and 1 ≤ w ≤ 1,000
Parallel roads between the same towns are allowed
hints: Recomputing all shortest paths after every new road would cost O(n<sup>3</sup>) each time, up to 100 times over. Is the old distance table still useful?
Keep the all-pairs matrix d. A shortest route in the new graph either ignores the new road (old value) or uses it exactly once, as a to b or b to a.

For a new road (a, b, w): for every pair (i, j) set d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][a] + w + d[b][j], d[i][b] + w + d[a][j]), reading the old values of rows a and b (copy them first). That is O(n2) per road; then add up the matrix again.
editorial: Run Floyd-Warshall once on the initial graph in O(n3). After that, adding an edge can be handled by one extra 'relaxation through the new edge' step, a degenerate version of Floyd-Warshall's inner loop. A new shortest route in the enlarged graph uses the new road at most once (weights are positive, so a route that used it twice would contain a useless cycle). If it uses the road from a to b, its cost is d[i][a] + w + d[b][j] with old distances on both sides, and the opposite direction gives the second formula.

Both formulas must read distances from before this update, because after the update d[i][a] itself may have decreased and mixing old and new values could count the new road twice. Copy the rows of a and b before touching the matrix. The total cost is O(n3 + q · n2), with q at most 100 and n at most 60 this is under a million steps for the update phase, versus roughly twenty million if you re-ran Floyd-Warshall for every query. The sum itself is O(n2) per query as well.
